title: My Daily Routine
description: Wake up, pray, breakfast, work, the long lunch, the late evening — tell the shape of your ordinary day with eight core verbs, and hear how one verb changes its face for I, you, he, she, we and they.
approach: GPA Phase 2 — first simplified video. A day-in-the-life vlog is watched with pictures only, then the same verbs are heard in the full paradigm, then the learner narrates their own day in five sentences.
unlock_condition: Narrate your own day in ≥5 correct present-tense sentences and score ≥12/16 on the who-is-doing-it listening sort
can_do: Describe your ordinary day with eight core verbs
Conjugate the Gulf present tense for every person
Ask what someone does every day

grammar.title: One verb, eight faces: the Gulf present tense
grammar.explanation: In Gulf Arabic the present verb changes its beginning to show who is doing it: أ- is 'I' (أروح), تـ is 'you' and also 'she' (تروح), يـ is 'he' (يروح) and نـ is 'we' (نروح). Two endings finish the set: 'you (to a woman)' adds ـين (تروحين) and 'you all' and 'they' add ـون (تروحون، يروحون). This one form covers what you do every day and what you do in general — 'I drink coffee' and 'I drink coffee every morning' are the same word أشرب. Do not add a بـ in front for habits the way Egyptians do: in the Gulf بروح means 'I will go', which is a different lesson. In fast speech the vowel after تـ and نـ often vanishes, so تروح sounds like truuḥ and نروح like nruuḥ.

examples.english: I go to work every day
Do you (f) drink coffee in the morning?

culture.title: A day told by prayer times
culture.note: Ask a Gulf friend when something happens and the answer is often a prayer, not a clock: بعد الفجر (after dawn), بعد الظهر, بعد العصر, بعد المغرب, بعد العشا. The shape of the day follows: an early start, work or school until around two or three, then the real meal of the day — الغدا, lunch — at home with the family, followed by the afternoon lull when shops close and people nap. Life restarts after the sunset and evening prayers: malls stay open until midnight, visits begin at nine, dinner (العشا) is at ten or later. When you arrange anything, offer a prayer-time anchor and you will sound local.

phrases.english: After the afternoon prayer, God willing
After the evening prayer we go out

vocabulary.teaching_note: The first verb of any day-in-the-life vlog. Saudis and Kuwaitis both say أصحى; you will also hear أقوم ('I get up') for the same moment. Never the MSA أستيقظ.
vocabulary.image_scene: A person sitting up in bed stretching, sunlight through a curtain, an alarm clock showing 6:00.

example.english: I wake up at six every day

vocabulary.video_hint: The opening of a morning-routine vlog: alarm, bed, the vlogger saying أصحى / صحيت.

vocabulary.teaching_note: Same across the Arab world, so a free win — and the verb the coffee culture runs on. The prefix أ- is the 'I' marker you will now see on every verb in this lesson.
vocabulary.image_scene: A hand lifting a small glass of tea to the mouth, steam rising.

example.english: I drink coffee in the morning

vocabulary.video_hint: Someone pouring or sipping tea or coffee while narrating their morning.

vocabulary.teaching_note: The 'I' prefix meets a hamza and becomes a long aa: آكل aakil, not a-akul. 'He eats' is ياكل yaakil — the same stretched vowel.
vocabulary.image_scene: A person eating rice from a plate with their right hand at a low family table.
vocabulary.video_hint: A family meal in a vlog; the vlogger saying آكل / ناكل as food is on screen.

vocabulary.teaching_note: The most-used verb in the dialect. Gulf 'go' is راح, never the MSA ذهب — أذهب will mark you as reading from a textbook. Place follows directly: أروح السوق, no 'to' needed.
vocabulary.image_scene: A person walking out of a front door with car keys, a white SUV in the driveway.

example.english: I go to work at seven

vocabulary.video_hint: Leaving the house or getting into a car; 'أروح' or 'نروح' said as the destination is named.

vocabulary.teaching_note: Gulf 'work' as a verb is اشتغل; the noun for the working day is الدوام. Both appear constantly in job talk. Note the غ in the middle — a soft gargled g.
vocabulary.image_scene: A person at an office desk typing on a laptop, a name badge on the shirt.

example.english: I work from eight to four

vocabulary.video_hint: Workplace or commute footage; the vlogger explaining what they do — أشتغل في…

vocabulary.teaching_note: Notice the i in the middle: adris, not adrus. Students say أدرس for both 'I study' and 'I am a student at'.
vocabulary.image_scene: A student at a desk with open books and a laptop, a university building through the window.
vocabulary.video_hint: Study-with-me vlogs; a student describing their day at university.

vocabulary.teaching_note: Long aa in the middle. The afternoon nap after lunch is a real institution, so you will hear أنام شوي ('I sleep a bit') in the middle of the day, not only at night.
vocabulary.image_scene: A person asleep in bed, room dark, phone face-down on the bedside table.
vocabulary.video_hint: The end of a day-in-the-life vlog; lights off, أنام or تصبحون على خير.

vocabulary.teaching_note: The homecoming verb — 'I get back from work' is أرجع من الدوام. Ends in ع, the deep throat sound; hold it rather than dropping it.
vocabulary.image_scene: A person walking back in through the front door in the afternoon, bag over shoulder.

example.english: I come back home at four

vocabulary.video_hint: Arriving home in a vlog; 'رجعت البيت' or 'أرجع' as the door opens.

vocabulary.teaching_note: Five times a day, so it anchors every routine. The prayer name follows directly: أصلي الفجر, أصلي المغرب. Doubled ل — hold it.
vocabulary.image_scene: A prayer mat laid out facing a wall, a person standing on it in prayer.

example.english: I pray Fajr and go back to sleep

vocabulary.video_hint: A vlogger mentioning prayer as a time marker — بعد ما أصلي — or a mosque visit.

vocabulary.teaching_note: Gulf 'see' and 'watch' are the same verb, شاف — never the MSA أرى. Saudis also say أطالع for watching; أتابع is 'I follow' a show.
vocabulary.image_scene: A family on a sofa watching a large TV in the evening, tea glasses on the table.
vocabulary.video_hint: Evening scenes with a TV or phone on; أشوف / نشوف said about a show or match.

vocabulary.teaching_note: كل is pronounced kill in the Gulf, not kull. Put it at the start or the end of the sentence — both are natural. It is the phrase that turns a verb into a habit.
vocabulary.image_scene: A wall calendar with every day of the week ticked in green.

example.arabic: كل يوم أشرب شاي بعد الغدا
example.transliteration: kill yoom ashrab shaay baʿd il-ghada
example.english: Every day I drink tea after lunch

vocabulary.video_hint: Routine narration — 'كل يوم أصحى…' — at the start of a day vlog.

vocabulary.teaching_note: Gulf speakers do use this word, often written عادة online. غالباً ('mostly') is the close cousin. Be careful: the same letters without the ending, عادي, means 'normal / no big deal' — a very different word you will meet constantly.
vocabulary.image_scene: A weekly planner with the same coffee-cup icon drawn in most, but not all, of the mornings.

example.english: Usually I have lunch at three

vocabulary.video_hint: A vlogger explaining a habit — عادةً أروح… — with the activity on screen.

vocabulary.teaching_note: A true Gulf marker: the meal is الريوق and the verb is تريّق. Saudis in the west say أفطر (from فطور); both are heard, but ريوق is what tells a listener you learned the dialect from people, not books.
vocabulary.image_scene: A breakfast spread of flatbread, eggs, cheese, dates and a glass of tea on a floor cloth.

example.english: I have eggs and bread for breakfast

vocabulary.video_hint: Breakfast in a morning vlog; the word ريوق or فطور as the food is shown.

vocabulary.teaching_note: Lunch is الغدا, the main meal, and it has its own verb. تغديت؟ ('have you had lunch?') even works as a greeting in the afternoon.
vocabulary.image_scene: A large platter of kabsa in the middle of a family sitting on the floor at midday.

example.english: I have lunch at home with my family

vocabulary.video_hint: Midday family meal; الغدا named, or the greeting تغديت؟

vocabulary.teaching_note: Dinner is العشا and comes late — ten at night is normal. The verb pairs with أتغدى; learn them together. Note the doubled ش.
vocabulary.image_scene: A late-night table with grilled meat and bread, a clock on the wall showing 10:00.

example.english: I have dinner late, at ten

vocabulary.video_hint: Evening restaurant or home dinner; العشا said as the food arrives.

vocabulary.teaching_note: Everyone drives, so this is a daily-routine verb in the Gulf. ق is g: asuug. Do not confuse with السوق (the market) — same letters, related idea of 'driving' goods, different word.
vocabulary.image_scene: Hands on a steering wheel, a wide sunny highway ahead, dashboard visible.

example.english: I drive to work every day

vocabulary.video_hint: In-car footage in a vlog; the driver narrating أسوق / نسوق.

sound_spotlight.explanation: After the 'you/she' تـ and the 'we' نـ, Gulf speakers usually drop the vowel, so تروح is truuḥ in one beat, not ti-ruuḥ. Listen for the consonant cluster at the start; it is one of the things that makes Gulf sound fast.

The feminine 'you' and the plural endings carry a long vowel and the stress moves onto them: tishra-BIIN, yruu-ḤUUN. Gulf keeps these endings always — there is no dropping of the ن as in formal Arabic.
When the 'I' prefix meets a verb that starts with hamza, the two merge into one long aa: آكل, آخذ. You will see the madda (آ) in captions; hear it as a held vowel.

lesson_sequence.detail: A 60-second day-in-the-life clip plays with no text — the learner just watches a Gulf morning unfold: alarm, prayer mat, breakfast, car. One English line: today you learn to tell your day.
Sixteen cards, each with its illustration and native audio in the 'I' form. Tap to hear the 'he' and 'you' forms underneath.
The paradigm table for أروح builds row by row with audio; then the learner drags pronouns onto blank verb forms for أشرب and أشتغل.
Listening sort: sixteen short clips (أروح، تروحين، ينامون…) sorted into I / you / he / she / we / they buckets. Immediate feedback with the ending highlighted.
The same 60-second clip now with Gulf captions; the learner taps every verb they recognise. Recognised verbs light up in the paradigm table.
Five prompts (wake up, breakfast, go to, come back, night) — the learner records one sentence each. Fluency feedback, no grading beyond verb form.
Words-learned counter rolls up. Nudge: tomorrow, narrate your morning in your head in Gulf as you do it.

real_world_prompts.prompt: Tomorrow morning, say each step out loud as you do it: أصحى… أشرب قهوة… أتريق… أروح الدوام.
real_world_prompts.context: Next-morning notification. Activates the routine verbs in the here-and-now while the actions are happening.

real_world_prompts.prompt: Ask a Gulf friend or tutor: شنو تسوي كل يوم؟ — and listen for the prayer times they use as clock markers.
real_world_prompts.context: Shown on the lesson-complete screen; a tutor-ready question that elicits the whole paradigm in the answers.

real_world_prompts.prompt: Find a day-in-the-life vlog and count how many times you hear أروح / نروح. Write the number down.
real_world_prompts.context: Optional homework card. Passive recognition of the highest-frequency verb in authentic speech.
